tag: Episode 27 Side Story · The One Who Stays
title: The One Who Stays

beats.t: The night before the door opened. All the bakery lights were out; only the oven breathed low.
Yundal sat alone before it. A sheet of yellow paper and a brush rested on his knees. Three layers of bandage covered the hole spreading to his wrist.
All right, dear customer. Last service of the day.
No customers. Since people had begun forgetting him, half his speech was to himself. He was used to it.
His brush wrote the lady's Day Pillar, 乙亥. He drew eight little stars around it and left the last one empty.
A talisman is strongest when used only once. Try to use it twice, and greed gets into it.
He held the finished talisman to the firelight and nodded with satisfaction.
A wayfinding talisman. It lights her road back once. No expiry, no refunds.
What are you doing there?
Oh, Mr. Cat. Customer Support patrols at night, too.
I followed the smell. Ink.
Neo looked at the talisman, then the bandage beneath it. Black stains seeped through its edge.
That's for Yeoni?
I'll slip it into her bread bag tomorrow morning. Give it directly, and she'll thank me. Then I might cry.
You don't cry.
You don't know me at all, Mr. Cat. I cry easily. People just forget that part.
Neo didn't answer. He sat beside Yundal, and for a while they watched the oven together.
You knew you couldn't cross the door?
Since I first fell here. You can't return without your hour. In three years, I've reached that door twice.
Both times...
Yes. Both times, the door failed to recognize me.
I wasn't alone at first. Someone else got the app that same day. They disappeared before I did.
By the time I went looking, it was too late. I'm always one step behind.
A log collapsed in the oven, scattering sparks. Yundal caught one in his bandaged hand. The hole swallowed it.
I'll stay beside Yeoni over there. Hold on here.
Of course. Holding on is the one thing I'm good at.
And thank you. For the river last night.
Wow. A thank you from Mr. Cat. Put that on a talisman and it'd sell out.
I take it back.
The following morning, the door opened. Golden wind filled the bakery storeroom.
As the lady crossed the threshold, Yundal murmured a name. Not Yundal. He hoped perhaps the person crossing might carry it through for him.
The wind covered it. She seemed about to turn, but the door was already closing.
Too much to hope for, I suppose.
It became an old storeroom door again. Over sooner than expected. Yundal stood there a long time, then brushed the handle once. Still warm.
Around noon, Moka packed: just a bundle of skewer rods and the ember jar filled yesterday.
Off to the festival island, then. Need a boat before the embers cool.
Take care, Mr. Otter. Cut back on the rapping, too.
I'm not cutting back the rap. And fraud, if you're going to mope, do it on the festival island.
Sit by the fire there, and I'll give you skewers.
Free?
On credit.
Cradling the jar, Moka ran for the dock without looking back. Yundal could wave freely until the otter's tail vanished at the alley's end.
That night, he spread paper on a corner table. White paper, the yellow talisman sheets set aside.
He dipped his brush and wrote a name. Not Yundal, but the name he'd written under his home address until three years ago.
Before the ink dried, the edges blurred. Stroke by stroke, the letters sank into the paper and vanished. With the last gone, the sheet was white again.
A little fast today.
He wrote again. It vanished again. The third time, he set the brush down and read the name aloud.
As soon as it became sound, it scattered among bread smells and oven smoke. It reached no one's ears.
It's all right. I remember.
He didn't know whether it really was all right. But over three years, he had learned very well how to say it.
Mister, aren't you sleeping?
Ah, Miss Luna. You're awake?
I was thirsty. What's your name, mister?
Sis told me to ask this morning. She says a new guest keeps hanging around.
Yundal's face stiffened for an instant. A new guest. Not words he'd expected from someone who'd baked beside him yesterday.
Yundal. A month that's there and not there. A name it's all right to forget.
Mr. Yundal! Got it! I'll tell Sis tomorrow.
Thank you. Then please ask me again tomorrow.
Yawning, Luna returned to her room. Yundal watched her for a long time. Tomorrow morning, that child would ask again. Mister, what's your name?
He went into the alley and looked up. Where Black Moon had been driven away, the sky's crack was closed, but not completely.
Starlight from another world leaked through. Strange stars stood in twelve rows, each row holding one great star whose name he didn't know.
Another sky.
The hole in his palm pulled toward that light by itself. Since the day it formed, it had always leaned toward Black Moon.
There you are. The master of the thing that ate my time.
He pulled his glove firmly back over the bandage.
She'll come back if she uses the talisman. She's not someone who forgets good bread.
Then I'll go ahead and secure a place. Location matters for a compatibility booth.
Mr. Cat will get jealous again. That helps business, too.
When Luna's sister opened the bakery next morning, the corner table was empty. Beside a brush, a white sheet lay with nothing written on it.
Who left paper here?
Luna's sister folded it and put it in a drawer. She did not throw it away. She didn't know why, either.
